analysis.one_liner: Extends the patent monopoly on a specific anti-inflammatory drug because FDA approval took years.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have lengthened a drug patent because FDA review took about six and a half years, was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have extended the patent on a specific non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (a pain and inflammation medicine). The patent holder filed for FDA approval in 1982 and waited at least 78 months before approval in 1991, so the bill would add most of that waiting time back onto the patent's life. A longer patent means the brand-name maker keeps exclusive sales rights for years longer, delaying cheaper generic competition. The bill never got past the committee referral stage.
analysis.who_benefits: The patent holder for the specific drug covered by the bill's criteria (a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory whose FDA application was filed in 1982, took at least 78 months, and was approved in 1991). The extension adds back the FDA review time minus 790 days, giving the company extra years of exclusive, monopoly-priced sales [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Extends the patent term for any patent covering a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug whose FDA new drug application was filed in 1982, took at least 78 months, and was approved in 1991 [S2][S3].
The extension equals the time the drug's application was pending at FDA, minus 790 days, restoring marketing time lost to regulatory review [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers and health plans, who would keep paying brand-name prices for the drug for years longer instead of switching to cheaper generics once the patent expired as scheduled [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: A longer patent delays generic competition, so patients and insurers pay monopoly prices for the drug for years beyond the original expiration date [S2][S3].

The bill is tailored so narrowly (a 1982 filing, at least 78 months of review, 1991 approval) that it covers essentially one drug, granting a targeted benefit rather than a general rule; supporters would argue the innovator genuinely lost patent life to an unusually long FDA review and deserves compensation [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The rationale is real: FDA review consumed years of the patent's life, and patent law generally allows some restoration for regulatory delay. But this bill is a bespoke extension for one product, and its cost falls on patients who would pay brand-name prices for extra years. Whether the compensation formula (pending time minus 790 days) is fair depends on facts the record does not provide; as written, its main guaranteed effect is a longer monopoly for the patent holder.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when that Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 9, 1992, by Rep. William Clay with 11 cosponsors from both parties [S1][S3][S4].
It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day, and no further action was taken for the rest of the Congress [S5].
The 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, so the bill expired without a committee vote or floor action [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers and generic drug makers, who would have faced years of continued monopoly pricing on the drug had the patent extension passed; the bill died quietly in committee, so the patent expired as scheduled.

for.name: Rep. William (Bill) Clay
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to extend the patent term for the covered anti-inflammatory drug

for.name: 11 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Jack Brooks, D-TX)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 9, 1992 and never scheduled a markup or vote, letting the bill die at the end of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor was a Democrat and its 11 cosponsors included 7 Republicans and 4 Democrats, so the push for the patent extension was bipartisan; there is no record of organized opposition because it never advanced.

industries.industry: Brand-name drug maker (patent holder for the covered anti-inflammatory)
industries.note: The bill would have added years of patent-exclusive sales, letting the company keep charging monopoly prices after the patent was otherwise set to expire [S2][S3].
Every extra year of patent life delays the day generic versions can enter and drive prices down, so generic makers lose sales the bill would have handed to the brand-name holder [S2].

industries.industry: Patients and health plans paying for the drug
industries.note: Consumers and insurers would bear the cost as higher drug prices during the extended patent term [S2].
